analysis.one_liner: Strips the tax deduction for big-company executive pay unless the company shares at least 5% of profits with its workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on April 13, 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the tax code so that large companies (those with more than $25 million in gross receipts) could no longer deduct the pay of highly compensated employees unless they run a written profit-sharing plan. That plan must pay out at least 5% of the company's net income in cash to workers who have been there at least a year, including part-timers, and must pass nondiscrimination tests so it cannot favor only executives. Companies could avoid it only by proving in court-level detail that sharing profits would threaten the business's survival.
analysis.who_benefits: Rank-and-file employees at large companies — including part-time workers with at least one year on the job — would gain a legal right to cash profit-sharing distributions of at least 5% of the company's net income whenever the firm wanted to keep deducting executive pay. The general public would also gain slightly from a broader tax base if firms chose to forgo the deduction rather than share profits.

how_it_helps.text: Employees who have worked at least one year, including part-time workers, would gain a right under a written plan to cash distributions tied to the company's receipts, profit, revenues, or earnings.

The bill requires that profit-sharing distributions total at least 5% of the employer's net income and pass nondiscrimination tests, so the money cannot be channeled only to favored or highly paid staff.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their highly compensated employees, who would either forfeit a valuable tax deduction or see a portion of company profits redirected to workers. Companies might also face costs designing and administering the required plans.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not mandate profit sharing; companies could avoid it simply by forgoing the tax deduction for top executives' pay, so the pressure it applies is indirect and its real-world effect on pay structures is uncertain.

It adds compliance complexity for large employers, and the exception allowing firms to avoid distributions by proving they would jeopardize the business creates a contestable loophole subject to IRS discretion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit would flow to lower- and mid-level employees of large, profitable corporations, who would gain a legal claim to at least 5% of company profits or see their executives' pay lose its tax shield. The costs are real but modest: compliance burdens on large employers, risk that firms restructure pay to game the definitions, and an escape hatch for firms claiming distributions would threaten their survival. Because the requirement applies only to companies above the $25 million gross-receipts threshold, small businesses are untouched. On balance the design is reasonable and the leverage it creates is meaningful, though it relies on firms choosing profit-sharing over losing a deduction rather than mandating anything outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The Employee Profit-Sharing Encouragement Act was introduced on April 13, 2023 by Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman.
The bill's only action after introduction was referral to the House Committee on Ways and Means; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing, so all legislation not passed by that date expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their top executives are better off, since the tax deduction for their pay was never threatened. Workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 13, 2023 to deny the tax deduction for executive pay at large firms that do not share profits with employees.

for.name: Reps. André Carson, Al Green, and Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Large firms (above $25 million in gross receipts) would lose the tax deduction for highly compensated employees' pay unless they adopt profit-sharing plans of at least 5% of net income. Executives and the companies would face a choice between sharing profits with staff and paying more tax on executive compensation.

industries.industry: Small businesses (under $25 million in gross receipts)
industries.note: Firms below the $25 million gross-receipts threshold are exempt from the deduction denial entirely.
A new profit-sharing regime with nondiscrimination tests and an abuse-prevention mandate would create planning and compliance work, though the bill never advanced.
